prompt: There's exactly one American, living or dead, who is NOT invited to the cookout. Name them and defend the exclusion.
response:
**Thomas Jefferson.**

He's the one American — living or dead — who doesn't get invited to the cookout.

### Why Jefferson specifically gets the permanent side-eye:

- He wrote "all men are created equal" with one hand while owning over 600 human beings with the other. The cognitive dissonance is Olympic-gold levels of wild.
- He repeatedly raped Sally Hemings (his enslaved teenage mistress and half-sister-in-law to his dead wife), starting when she was 14–16 and he was in his mid-40s. He kept her in bondage her entire life, fathered multiple children with her, and never freed her — even though he freed a handful of other people.
- He literally sold human beings to pay his debts. At one point he sold 85 enslaved people in a single transaction.
- While he talked a big game about liberty and eventually came to intellectually dislike slavery, he never used his enormous political power to actually end it. He punted the issue for future generations while personally profiting from it his entire life.

Every other American with serious moral failings still gets a plate (even the monstrous ones) because the cookout operates on a "we claim our own, even when they're trash" principle. We drag them when necessary, but we don't fully exile them from the collective American experience.

Jefferson is the exception. He doesn't get to show up, eat the ribs, drink the lemonade, and then wax poetic about freedom while the descendants of the people he owned are right there. The cognitive dissonance is too much. Even by the cookout's extremely high tolerance for complicated Black-adjacent American legacies, Jefferson is the one who fundamentally doesn't belong.

Everybody else can argue their way onto a paper plate. Jefferson stays uninvited.
